(2) It casts the most expensive castable spell: the greatest mana spent now (reductions and commander tax counted, a free cast is 0), then the printed mana value, then its PRNG, and repeats at the next priority until nothing castable is left, since the engine lists only what the remaining mana can pay. This is "dearest first", not the set of spells that uses the most mana (PRIOR_ART heuristic 8 is for the `HeuristicAgent`). Spells that need a target that does not exist are skipped by the casual `worthCasting`, because a cast cannot be cancelled safely. No flashback, escape, suspend, activations or regeneration: it passes. (3) Attack: a creature with power attacks when it SURVIVES: no untapped creature of the opponent that could block it (flying, reach, fear, intimidate, shadow, landwalk and "can't block" read from the view) kills it alone, where a blocker kills when its damage (twice its power with double strike) reaches the attacker's remaining toughness or it has deathtouch, an indestructible attacker cannot be killed, and a first striker that would kill a blocker without first strike takes no damage; a menace attacker is judged against each pair of potential blockers. Gang blocks by creatures that cannot kill it alone are not assumed, and an even trade is not survival, so the creature stays home. A creature that must attack is declared. If the attack is lethal it sends everything: each untapped potential blocker group stops one of the biggest attackers it can block, biggest first (menace takes two), and if what is left reaches the opponent's life, ten poison, or 21 commander damage from a commander (the view keys commander damage by card, not object, so any damage the opponent took counts toward the clock), every candidate attacks. Attack taxes go through `payForAttacks`. (4) Blocks: only when the attackers at it that are unblocked would be lethal (life, poison, or a commander reaching 21); it then blocks, biggest threat first but preferring a block that already makes the rest survivable, with the cheapest creatures that can block (by mana value, ties by object id), until the rest is not lethal. Block taxes go through `withinBlockBudget`. (5) It pays with `payAuto` and never concedes.
- Decision, harness (`arena.ts`, `arena-decks.ts`): `playMatch({ a, b, decks, games, baseSeed, budget? })` plays `games` games (an even number) as `games / 2` seeds, each seed twice with the seats swapped, on the same game seed and the same deck, with the same list on both seats (a mirror). The game seed of pair `i` is `baseSeed + i`, the deck `decks[i % decks.length]`, and the agent seeds are derived from the game seed and equal in both games of a pair. The game seed fixes the shuffles, so both games deal the same cards to seat 0 and seat 1; the pairing balances seats and deals between the agents, but does not give an agent the same hand in both games. The result has wins per agent, wins per agent per seat, wins per seat, draws, games without a result (`unfinished`, kept apart from draws so a stalled agent shows), average turns, fallbacks, rejected actions and the reason histogram per agent. `ARENA_DECKS` are three fixed 24-card lists of real fixtures (no SYNTHETIC cards). `tools/ai/arena.ts` (`pnpm ai:arena`) runs it from the command line; its output names the command that reproduces it. `tools/package.json` gains the workspace dependency on `@commander-arena/ai`; no boundary rule changed (`pnpm lint:boundaries` scans `packages` and `apps`).
- Alternatives: An evaluator that scores one seat's strength only: rejected, a search needs one scale for both sides, and antisymmetry gives a testable relation. Choosing the set of spells that uses the most mana for `GreedyAgent`: rejected, A11 says "the most expensive castable spells" and the benchmark should stay simple; the set is the first upgrade of the `HeuristicAgent`. Playing a land and a spell by copying the casual priority handler: rejected, it also activates, flashes back and regenerates, which are not A11's rules. Counting each seed once with a coin flip for the seat: rejected, a pair removes the seat and deal luck from the comparison instead of averaging it out. Test decks from the games helpers (`test/helpers.ts`) for the harness: rejected, they live in the test directory and are generated per style; the harness needs fixed lists that `src` and the tool can both import.
- Measured (cloud machine, `pnpm ai:arena`, 200 games = 100 seeds from seed 1, each played twice with the seats swapped, no fallback and no rejected action in either run): `node tools/ai/arena.ts --a greedy --b random --games 200 --seed 1`: greedy 194 wins (97.0%; 96 from seat 0, 98 from seat 1), random 6, no draws, 19.4 turns on average. `node tools/ai/arena.ts --a casual --b greedy --games 200 --seed 1`: casual 144 wins (72.0%; 72 from each seat), greedy 56, no draws, 25.5 turns on average. So the A11 benchmark is weaker than the `CasualAgent` on these decks, and the `HeuristicAgent` has to beat a weaker target than the web opponent; the mirror and the 70% line are for M7c to measure.
- Consequences: `GreedyAgent` in a mirror tends to stall: both sides hold back creatures a blocker would kill. In a spot check of six greedy-against-greedy games on the arena decks (seeds 1 to 3, both seat orders) every game reached turn 60, the empty-library ending of 24-card decks; it is not a 200-game run. The `HeuristicAgent` must break such stalemates. A match takes seconds per game (about 4 s on the loaded cloud machine), so the 200-game runs are the `pnpm ai:arena` script, never a unit test (D-126); the unit tests play a handful of games. The evaluator's constants are not tuned. `casual-priority.ts` exports `landPlays`, `chooseLand`, `spellPlays`, `spendOf`, `withFace` and `Play` so `GreedyAgent` can reuse them; the agent files `agent.ts` and `runner.ts` are untouched.

## D-163: M7c: the HeuristicAgent, its rules, its tuning and its measured strength (2026-10-30)
- Context: M7 is done when `HeuristicAgent` beats `GreedyAgent` in 70% of 200 games, `RandomLegalAgent` in 95%, and mirrored self-play lands between 40% and 60% per seat (SPEC A11). The agent builds on M7a (`DecideContext.sample`, a determinized state to play forward, D-161) and M7b (the evaluator, reason codes, `GreedyAgent`, `playMatch`, D-162). The ideas come from the ranked table of `docs/PRIOR_ART.md` 7.2 (heuristics 1 to 3 and 5 to 10), restated in our own words; no XMage or Forge text or code was used and every test was written for this repository.
- Decision, structure (`packages/ai/src/heuristic-*.ts`, each under 400 lines): `HeuristicAgent({ seed, level?, name?, handlerOverrides? })` implements `ExplainingAgent`. It answers priority, targets, mulligan, attackers and blockers itself and every other decision kind with `createCasualHandlers`, so it handles every kind and cannot deadlock; a throwing handler falls back to the first safe legal action and is recorded as on the `CasualAgent`; each decision is recorded with a reason (`reasons.ts` gained the codes `good-block`, `trade-block`, `gang-block`, `sim-attack`, `crack-back`, `deck-race`, `keep`, `mulligan`, `land-fix`, `land-late`, `commander`, `removal`, `removal-attacker`, `trick`, `end-step`, `counter`, `hold`, `target-commander`, `target-best`). Its own seeded PRNG gives tie-breaks of the casual handlers, the seeds of the samples (`ctx.sample(seed)`) and the noise of Easy. It never reads a clock: `heuristic-budget.ts` stops a search when 60% of `ctx.budgetMs` has passed on `ctx.now` and takes the best candidate so far (the first two candidates of a decision are always scored). `MatchOptions.now` and `pnpm ai:arena --real-clock` pass a real clock for timing runs; win-rate runs use the runner's logical clock, so a result does not depend on the speed of the machine.
- Decision, combat on the sample (`heuristic-sim.ts`): a candidate is declared on the sample with `applyAction` and played to the end of combat with the engine (priority passes, the engine's default damage division, attack and block taxes paid with `payAuto`, other questions answered by the casual handlers with a fixed draw); a refused action drops the candidate, nothing is guessed. A property test (`heuristic-sim.test.ts`) shows that for random small boards (first strike, deathtouch, trample, lifelink, menace, indestructible, double strike, fliers) a random legal block played on the sample reaches the same public position as the real game with both seats passing.
- Decision, blocks (`heuristic-blockplan.ts`, `heuristic-blocks.ts`, `heuristic-danger.ts`, `heuristic-duel.ts`): candidate plans in tiers: (1) good blocks, the cheapest blocker (by `creatureValue`) that survives and kills when one does, else survives; (2) value trades (both die, the attacker is worth at least the blocker); (3) gang blocks of two that kill an attacker while it can kill only one of them, and the pairs a menace attacker needs; (4) chump blocks only while the damage that gets through leaves the agent in danger, strongest attacker first, with the blocker that makes the rest safe. Plans: no block, tiers 1, 1+2 and 1+2+3 each with and without the chump fill, the chump fill alone, and block-everything when the danger does not go away. Danger: life left at most 6, poison of 7 or more, one commander's damage of 15 or more (`DANGER_LIFE`, `DANGER_POISON`, `DANGER_COMMANDER`); lethal at the life total, ten poison (CR 704.5c) or 21 commander damage (CR 704.6c). What gets past is computed by `breakthrough` (each blocker stops one attacker, a menace attacker takes two, trample sends its excess over, double strike counts twice). Each plan, after the block tax is applied, is scored by `evaluate` from the agent's seat on the state at the end of combat; a block must beat no block by 0.05. Without a sample the deepest tier with its chump fill is taken.
- Decision, attacks (`heuristic-attacks.ts`): (1) the lethal check: each untapped potential blocker stops one of the biggest attackers it can block; if what is left is lethal every creature that can attack does (`lethal`). (2) Otherwise the candidates are none, the safe attackers (`survivesAttack` of GreedyAgent), every attacker, the attackers nothing can block, each of the three most valuable creatures alone, and with an opposing planeswalker the safe attackers at it; creatures that must attack are in every candidate and each candidate is trimmed by `payForAttacks` before it is simulated, so the declaration is final and the tax prompt is answered `payAuto` (no declined payment can repeat). Each is played out and scored by `evaluate` (with the agent's own creatures untapped, since they untap before it matters) minus a crack-back penalty: all the opponent's creatures attack, the agent's untapped ones block, and what gets through costs half the life value it takes, plus 3 in danger, or 400 when lethal (`CRACK_WEIGHT` 0.5). An attack must beat staying home by 0.05; ties go to fewer attackers. Targets: every attacker goes at the opposing player (the only opponent in v1 is the controller of the opposing commander); planeswalkers only through the one candidate above, scored like any other; battles are never attacked. (3) The opponent is not assumed to block perfectly: a candidate is played out twice, against an opponent that blocks sensibly (the block planner above) and one that blocks only in danger, and its numbers are the average weighted by `passiveWeight` (`heuristic-model.ts`): the share of the SENSIBLE blocks the agent has been offered in its own attacks (a blocker that survives, or a trade for an attacker worth as much) that were not made, with one made and one missed as the prior, so 1/2 before anything is seen. Only the public combat of the view in the declare-blockers step of its own turn is read. (4) The library clock (`urgency`): a board that nobody can win is lost by the player who has to draw from an empty library first; from the agent's turn the opponent draws next, so it is behind when its library has fewer cards than an opponent's, and its urgency rises from 0 at 14 cards to 1 at none; the score of a candidate is then `raw - (1 - u) * crack + u * 1 * lifeLostByTheOpponent`, and the reason is `deck-race` when that changed the choice.
- Decision, evaluator (`evaluate.ts`): one new term, pressure: `10 * min(1, P / L)` where P is the power of the seat's creatures without defender and L the weakest opponent's life, so damage is worth more as a clock nears (with the concave life curve alone, a big board never saw a reason to attack a player at 40 life). It keeps the evaluator antisymmetric (the fast-check properties of `evaluate.test.ts` pass and two cases were added). No other constant was changed.
- Decision, main phase (`heuristic-mana.ts`, `heuristic-lands.ts`, `heuristic-main.ts`, `heuristic-targets.ts`, `heuristic-mulligan.ts`): the mana is estimated from the "{T}: Add" text of untapped permanents (colour-aware, `canPayAll`); the land is the one that lets the most mana of the hand be spent this turn, then the one that adds a colour the hand needs, then a tapped land over an untapped one, then a plain land, then by id; it waits for the second main phase (`land-late`) when nothing needs it, a creature can attack and no permanent says landfall. The spells are the SET that uses the most mana (ties: the most value, `creatureValue` for a creature, 4 more for a commander, 0.8 of the target's value for removal), among permanents, sorceries and removal with a worthwhile target; the first of it is cast (reducers and land-drop grants first, removal before creatures when its target is worth as much as the best creature of the set, Storm last) and the plan is made again at the next priority. The commander is a play like any other except at a tax of 4 or more (two casts): it is then cast only when the best other set spends less than half of the mana and `evaluate` is at least -8. Removal (destroy, exile, damage, bounce, shrink; one slot) skips a target that is already dying (damage marked is lethal, or another removal spell on the stack names it), that the spell cannot kill (indestructible, more toughness than the damage, persist without a -1/-1 counter, undying without a +1/+1 counter) or whose ward cost the agent cannot pay with the mana left; the rest are ranked by `creatureValue` (a planeswalker by loyalty) with the opposing commander first when its value is at least 80% of the best, ties by object id with a code-unit compare, a defender aims at the attackers first; burn goes at the player when it is lethal. A pump is aimed at the creature in the combat that is not winning its fight. Instants wait for windows: after blockers (every trick or removal candidate is cast on the sample and the turn is played out to the start of the next one, so effects that last until end of turn do not count; it is cast when it beats passing by 0.5, `trick` or `removal-attacker`), the opponent's end step (the set of instant-speed plays that uses the most mana, `end-step`) and in response to an opponent's spell of mana value 2 or more (a counterspell, `counter`); the mana they need stays untapped because the main-phase set does not count them. What is left (flashback, escape, suspend and foretell, activated abilities) is the casual rules. Mulligan: keep with 2 to 5 lands and, before any mulligan, a spell of mana value at most the lands in hand plus one; otherwise take a mulligan while allowed and the hand after it keeps at least 5 cards (`keep`, `mulligan`).
- Decision, levels: `normal` is everything above. `easy` considers at most three block candidates (no block, the default plan, the deepest plan) and three attack candidates (none, safe, all), takes the second best of the scored candidates one time in four (its own PRNG), plays its mana like the `CasualAgent` (its land, its dearest spell, no set planning, no windows, no trick simulation), aims removal with the casual rule and keeps the same mulligan. Easy keeps the learned opponent model and the library clock. Measured numbers of Easy are below.
- Tuning log (all runs `node tools/ai/arena.ts ... --games 200 --seed 1` unless said; paired seeds, seats swapped, no fallback and no rejected action in any run): (a) the first complete agent (simulated blocks and attacks, crack-back, main-phase planning), against random 200 of 200, against casual 124 (62.0%), against greedy 126 (63.0%, target NOT met), mirror 100 each (seat 0 won 102). A look at 16 games (seed 1 to 8, both seats, against Greedy) showed why: 11 of them were stalls that ended at turn 34 with both libraries empty, which the player who draws first from the empty library loses, and which seat that is decides them, so a stall is a coin flip in a paired run; the agent won all 5 games that were not stalls (a sample, not a rate). (b) Two changes aimed at stalls: the pressure term and a boolean "the opponent is passive" flag from the block model: 39 of 60 (65.0%, seed 1, 60 games). (c) The library clock added: 45 of 60 (75.0%). (d) The model as a probability, with the attack candidates played out against both opponents and averaged: 55 of 60 (91.7%). Nothing else was tried in between; no seed was chosen: seed 1 is the harness default and seed 2 was run once, after the code was frozen. The honest summary: without the library clock and the opponent model the target against Greedy was not met (63.0%); both exist because the arena decks end in stalls, and both are tuned on them (ROADMAP).
- Measured (cloud machine, loaded by other jobs; the code of commit `7d91af5`, after which only tests and docs changed; `node tools/ai/arena.ts --a <a> --b <b> --games 200 --seed <n>`, 100 seeds each played twice with the seats swapped, logical clock; no fallback, no rejected action, no draw and no unfinished game in any run). Seed 1: `heuristic` against `greedy` 181 wins (90.5%; 90 from seat 0, 91 from seat 1; target 70% met), against `random` 200 (100.0%; target 95% met), mirror `heuristic` against `heuristic` 100 each (48 and 52 from seat 0 and seat 1 for each; wins of seat 0 96, of seat 1 104; target 40% to 60% met), against `casual` 123 (61.5%; the web opponent today). Seed 2: against greedy 184 (92.0%), against random 200 (100.0%), mirror 100 each (seat 0 won 98, seat 1 102), against casual 121 (60.5%). `heuristic-easy` (seed 1): against greedy 167 (83.5%), against casual 116 (58.0%), and `heuristic` against `heuristic-easy` 119 (59.5%). The first full run of the agent before the stall work, for comparison, is in the tuning log. Average game length: 22.7 to 23.1 turns against greedy (the greedy-against-greedy spot check of D-162 was 60), 28 to 29 against casual.
- Measured, decision time (the wrapper of `tools/ai/arena.ts` around `decide`, in the same runs, on the loaded machine): `heuristic` mean 1.9 to 3.4 ms and slowest 245 to 585 ms over the runs of both seeds, `heuristic-easy` mean 1.2 to 1.5 ms and slowest 124 to 164 ms; the budget is 1000 ms (SPEC 9). With a real clock (`--real-clock`, `heuristic` against `casual`, 40 games, seed 1: 26 wins of 40) the mean was 3.2 ms and the slowest 316.7 ms and the 60% cut-off never had to fire. The cut-off is proved by a fake-clock test (`heuristic-agent.test.ts`): a search that is already over the share reads the clock twice and answers; one that is not reads it more. These are decisions on 24-card arena decks; a board with 30 creatures a side was not timed.
- Alternatives: Choosing blocks and attacks by hand rules only (as GreedyAgent): rejected, the engine already resolves first strike, deathtouch, trample and the rest, and a simulation reuses it (the property test shows the sample plays them the same). Scoring attacks against one assumed opponent: rejected after the first measurement (63.0% against Greedy, which blocks only to prevent lethal and so is never punished for it); an agent that learns how the opponent blocks also fits a human who does not block, and costs two simulations per candidate. A stall-breaking rule on the turn number: rejected, the library clock says why a player must act. An evaluator term for the library: rejected, a static term cannot make "do nothing" lose; the clock is a rule of the attack choice. A knapsack over all spells including instants for the main phase: rejected for the instants, whose mana must stay open for their windows. Probing attacks to teach the model: not needed once attacks are averaged over both opponents. A test that Heuristic never reads hidden information through the sample: the sample is built by the host from the real state and `determinize` is tested in M7a; the agent receives only the view and the sample, so no extra check was added.
- Consequences: M7's exit criterion is met on the arena decks with seeds 1 and 2, with the two stall rules above, which are tuned on 24-card decks that end by decking; in a 100-card game they hardly fire. A game takes about as long as with the `CasualAgent` (mean decision a few milliseconds). `evaluate` has one new term, and `reasons.ts` many new codes (the Greedy and arena tests only list codes that occur). `MatchOptions.now` is new. The web app is untouched: wiring `HeuristicAgent`, the Easy and Normal setting and the real `now` are M7d. Known limits are in `docs/ROADMAP.md` (AI). No `ENGINE_VERSION` change: no rule changed.
- Status: The Easy level (`level: 'easy'`, `heuristic-easy`) was removed by D-168; the agent has one level, which plays as Normal did. Everything below about Easy is history; the tuning and the measurements of Normal stand.

## D-164: M7d: the web opponent is the HeuristicAgent, with an Easy and Normal setting, and it is measured on the real precons (2026-10-30)
- Context: M7a to M7c built `determinize`, the evaluator, the harness and the `HeuristicAgent` (D-161 to D-163); the web game still played the `CasualAgent` through a Worker host that gave it no real clock. SPEC 9 asks for Easy and Normal, a time budget of 1 s a decision and a short delay so a human can follow. The agent had been tuned and measured only on the 24-card arena decks, which end by decking; the web plays the 100-card precons.
- Decision, wiring: `NewGameOptions.ai` (`'casual' | 'easy' | 'normal'`, `game/protocol.ts`) names the opponent; the Worker host builds it with `createAgent(seed, kind)` (`game/agents.ts`): `easy` and `normal` are `HeuristicAgent` at that level, `casual` is the `CasualAgent`. The host's default for an absent field is `casual`, so a host built as in the existing tests behaves as before; the page always sets the field. The Worker's clock is `performance.now` (`worker.ts`), passed as `ctx.now` with the budget of 1000 ms (`DEFAULT_BUDGET_MS`); `ctx.sample` is the host's `determinize` (D-161). `HeuristicAgent` reads time only through `ctx.now` (the lint plugin bans `Date.now` and `performance.now` in `packages/ai/src`; a host test drives it with a fake clock that moves on every read and checks that no answer is replaced). The A28 watchdog is unchanged: an answer more than 500 ms past the budget is replaced by the safe fallback and counted. The host adds no delay after an AI action (it never did): the page shows the plays from the steps of the snapshot and the autopilot already waits 160 ms before an automatic pass of the human; SPEC 9's "short, configurable delay" for the AI's plays is not built (ROADMAP).
- Decision, the setting: `AiLevel` is `'easy' | 'normal'`, Normal by default. It lives where the next game is configured, on the menu (beside the seed, the free mulligan and the theme) and on the "Play this deck" panel of the import screen (`ui/panels/AiLevelPicker.tsx`, the logic and the storage in `ui/panels/ai-level.ts`, key `commander-arena.ai-level`, read when the app starts and wrapped in try/catch like the text size, so the page works without storage). It is not in the in-game Settings menu: that menu holds what can change during a game (stops, theme, text size, side, concede) and the level is fixed when the game starts, so a control there would either do nothing or change the opponent in the middle of a game. Each level has a plain hint under the picker: "Easy: plays more simply and sometimes misses its best play." and "Normal: plans blocks and attacks by looking ahead." The menu and `playReport` copy the setting into `NewGameOptions.ai`. The replay export carries it in `options`.
- Decision, autostart and tests: `?autostart=<human>,<ai>&seed=<n>` plays `casual` unless `&ai=casual|easy|normal` names another agent (`game/autostart.ts`; a wrong value is ignored). The default stays `casual` on purpose: the end-to-end and unit tests were written against the `CasualAgent`'s play (seeded games reach exact situations), and they must not change with the player's setting or with the stronger agent. A menu start uses the setting. Tests added: the setting and its storage (including no storage and no window), what the menu, "Play this deck" and `startOptionsFor` put in the start message, the URL parsing, `createAgent`, the host asking for the kind of the message, the host handing the agent its budget and the host clock, the margin of A28 (kept at budget plus margin, replaced one millisecond later), the `HeuristicAgent` run through the host with fake clocks, and a Playwright file that starts a game from the menu with Normal and with Easy, presses the primary button for five turn banners and checks for no error toast, no page error and no "AI fallback" chip (`e2e/ai-level.e2e.ts`; the file also checks that the level is remembered and that `?autostart` with and without `&ai=` starts).
- Decision, time on big boards (found by the measurement below): the 60% cut-off is checked between candidates, and on a board of about 80 permanents (a late game of the Angels precon against the casual agent) one candidate play-out took 2.4 s, so one declare-blockers decision took 3.0 s; two decisions of the 200-game mirror run went past the 500 ms margin and would have been replaced by fallbacks in the web host. The engine's `derive` of static effects dominated the profile (`staticEffectsOn` and its callers took about half of the time, an engine cost per `applyAction` and `getView` on a big board, which is not changed here). Fixes in the agent: (1) `Budget.expired(done)` also stops when the next candidate, at the average cost of the `done` so far, would end past the 60% share; (2) `Budget.over()` is true from 70% of the budget (`HARD_SHARE`) and `SimPolicy.abort` makes `playOut` check it before every engine step and drop the candidate (null, like a refused action), so a play-out overruns by at most one step; the trick simulation of the main phase uses it too; (3) when fewer than two candidates were scored because a play-out ran out of time, the rules-based plan answers (the block plan or the safe attack that the agent gives without a sample), which handles danger and lethal by itself. The logical clock of the runner never moves inside a decision, so no win-rate run changes; the 40-game runs below gave the same win counts before and after.
- Decision, tools: `playMatch` takes, besides a `DeckConfig` (a mirror), a deck entry `[seat 0 deck, seat 1 deck]`; the decks stay with the seat when the agents swap, so each agent plays each deck once and each seat once. `node tools/ai/arena.ts --precons [--pairing mirror|cross]` builds the five precons of `apps/web/src/precons/snapshots/` with the web app's own modules (`createImportService`, `snapshotClient`, `checkPlayable`, as `buildPreconDeck` does; that file itself cannot load under Node because of its sibling's `import.meta.glob`), `mirror` giving both seats the same precon (one per pair index) and `cross` every ordered pair of two different precons; a precon the web would refuse is reported and left out. New flags: `--max-turns`, `--max-actions`, `--log-slow <ms>` (one line per slow decision with the agent seed, so a game can be found again); the timing report counts the decisions over the budget. `tools/ai/precons.test.ts` is the soak for CI: the five snapshots become 100-card decks, and eight games of `heuristic` against `heuristic-easy` on precon-against-precon pairs finish with no fallback and no rejected action (eight, not twenty, because a precon game takes about 2 to 3 s; the 20-game convention of D-126 is for the 24-card style games).
- Measured (cloud machine, other jobs running; the code after the fix above, all with `--real-clock`, so the budget is live; the decks `angels, artifacts, dinosaurs, dragons, zombies`, no fallback, no rejected action, no draw and no unfinished game in any run; "seat 0 and seat 1" are the wins of the agent in each seat). 40 games each (20 seeds from 1, `node tools/ai/arena.ts --precons --pairing <p> --a <a> --b <b> --games 40 --seed 1 --real-clock`): `heuristic` against `casual`, mirror: heuristic 22 (55.0%; 12 and 10), casual 18, 19.2 turns on average; cross: heuristic 22 (55.0%; 10 and 12), 15.6 turns. `heuristic-easy` against `casual`, mirror: easy 21 (52.5%; 11 and 10), 19.4 turns; cross: easy 17 (42.5%; 8 and 9), 15.5 turns. `heuristic` against `heuristic`, mirror: 20 each (10 and 10 each; seat 0 won 20, seat 1 won 20), 17.5 turns; cross: 20 each (7 and 13 each; seat 0 won 14, seat 1 won 26), 16.4 turns. 200 games of `heuristic` against `casual` (100 seeds from 101, so none of the seeds above; `--seed 101`): mirror 122 (61.0%; 52 as seat 0 and 70 as seat 1), casual 78, seat 0 won 82 and seat 1 won 118, 19.3 turns, 654 s; cross 114 (57.0%; 56 and 58), casual 86, seat 0 won 98 and seat 1 won 102, 17.0 turns, 381 s. Decision time (mean, slowest, decisions over 1000 ms): `heuristic` against `casual`, 40 games: mirror 3.64 ms, 651.1 ms, none; cross 2.71 ms, 612.2 ms, none; `heuristic` against `heuristic` (both agents pooled under one label): mirror 3.10 ms, 681.9 ms, none; cross 3.08 ms, 666.5 ms, none; `heuristic-easy` against `casual`: mirror 1.99 ms, 492.8 ms; cross 1.25 ms, 324.1 ms; `heuristic` against `casual`, 200 games: mirror 3.82 ms, 869.9 ms, none; cross 2.60 ms, 712.5 ms, none. The casual agent's slowest decision was 12.3 ms. Reason histogram, top entries of the 200-game mirror run: `no-play` 43756, `delegated` 4122, `curve` 1895, `land-fix` 979, `safe-attack` 513, `hold` 391, `land-late` 351, `commander` 340, `no-block` 276, `sim-attack` 276; of the cross run: `no-play` 37127, `delegated` 3169, `curve` 1526, `land-fix` 934, `safe-attack` 530, `commander` 268, `hold` 264, `land-late` 244, `keep` 200, `no-block` 196. Before the fix, the first 200-game mirror run (the same command, with `--log-slow 400`) had `heuristic` at 122 wins as well, 8 decisions over 1000 ms and a slowest of 2845.4 ms; the cross run 113 wins and one decision at 1351.2 ms; the 40-game mirror run had one decision at 1057.8 ms.
- Findings on the real precons: (1) the win rate against the casual agent is 55% to 61% over 40 and 200 games, against 60.5% to 61.5% on the arena decks (D-163): a smaller edge on the cross pairs (57.0% in 200 games), within what 40 games cannot tell apart (the standard error of 40 games is about 8 points, of 200 about 3.5). Nothing was tuned for it. (2) `heuristic-easy` is about even with the casual agent on the precons (52.5% and 42.5% in 40 games each, 58.0% on the arena decks): Easy is not clearly stronger than the old opponent on real decks, only simpler than Normal; the "Easy" hint says what it does, not that it is weak. (3) In a mirror between agents of one kind the two games of a seed are identical (the agent's seed does not change its play enough to matter: the winner, the seat and the turn count were the same in the five pairs checked), so wins per agent are 50% by construction and the informative number is the split by seat; this also holds for D-163's mirror numbers on the arena decks ("100 each"), whose 40% to 60% check therefore could not fail. The cross pairs differ by deck and show the deck-seat effect (seat 1 won 26 of 40 in the `heuristic` cross run). (4) The player on the draw wins more in the precon mirror (118 of 200 for seat 1 against the casual agent). (5) The decision times: mean a few milliseconds, slowest below the budget after the fix; before it, up to 2.8 s on boards of 70 to 80 permanents.
- Alternatives: Putting the difficulty in the in-game Settings menu: rejected, the level is fixed when the game starts. Making `normal` the default of the host for an absent field: rejected, it would change every host and end-to-end test that was written against the `CasualAgent`; the page sets the field in every start path. A new level name for the casual agent in the player's setting: rejected, it is a test seam. Moving the 60% cut-off earlier: rejected, the problem was the candidate that straddled the limit, not the limit. Making the engine's `derive` faster: the real fix for big boards, and a different slice (ROADMAP). Skipping the simulation above a number of permanents: rejected, a guess that the clock measures better. Importing the web's `build.ts` in the tool: not possible (`import.meta.glob`); loading the community definitions: not done, none ships.
- Consequences: The web game is playable against the agent that D-163 measured; the AI games take about as long as before (a few milliseconds a decision, 2 to 3 s for a whole precon game in the arena). On a board of 80 permanents a decision can still use about 700 ms plus one engine step and the answer may be the rules-based plan: the agent plays worse, never slower than the margin. A real clock makes the agent's answer depend on the speed of the machine in that case, so a replay of a game with a huge board could differ from the original (`exportReplay` replays the human's actions against a fresh host); a replay import is not built. The logs of `?autostart` games are unchanged. No `ENGINE_VERSION` change: no rule changed.
- Status: The Easy and Normal setting (`AiLevel`, `ui/panels/ai-level.ts`, `AiLevelPicker.tsx`, the localStorage key `commander-arena.ai-level`) and the `'easy'` kind of `NewGameOptions.ai` were removed by D-168; `ai` is `'casual' | 'normal'` and the menu and the import screen send `'normal'`. The rest of this entry stands.

## D-165: No player-facing save, load, resume or replay export or import (2026-10-30)
- Context: The owner simplified the product. Saves and replays (D-026, SPEC 17.6 A26) were planned for M9, and only the replay download on the game-over screen had been built; no load, resume or replay import existed.
- Decision: The app has no save, load, resume, replay export or replay import. The game-over screen lost its "Download replay" button, and the Worker protocol and the host lost `exportReplay` and the `ReplayExport` type. The seed stays for players (`?seed=` and the seed field of the menu). `replayGame` in `packages/ai`, the engine's action log and the seeded PRNG stay as a test tool: the AI game tests and the determinism scenario replay games through them.
- Alternatives: Keeping the export only: rejected, a file nothing can import is of no use to a player. Building the import and the saves: rejected by the owner, the product is simpler without them.
- Consequences: The determinism checks stay cheap and unchanged. The host tests that rebuilt a game from the exported log now compare two hosts fed the same seed and answers, and the view after an undo with the view before the move. SPEC A26, the replay export line of section 10, the M9 line and the replay file schema line of 17.6 are history; the SPEC collapse handles them.

## D-166: No support-request pipeline (2026-10-30)
- Context: The owner simplified the product. The app let a player turn an unsupported card into a support request (a request dialog with "Copy for agent" and "Download request", a dev-only "Send to inbox" endpoint that wrote `card-requests/inbox/`, a "Your requests" list in IndexedDB that marked requests resolved on later imports), and `pnpm card:request` built the same file from Scryfall. On 2026-10-30 the owner decided to remove the requested-card tracking and keep deck import and the unsupported flags.
- Decision: There is no support-request pipeline. Removed: the request dialog, the "Request support" buttons, the inbox button and its Vite plugin, the "Your requests" tab and menu button, the `requests` store of the web app, `packages/cards/src/requests/` (`CardSupportRequest`, `buildSupportRequest`, `validateRequest`, `agentMessage`), `pnpm card:request` (`tools/card-request/`) and the `card-requests/` directory. New cards to support come from the owner or from a GitHub issue, and the loop in `docs/CARD_SUPPORT_PLAYBOOK.md` starts there. Deck import, the Scryfall client and cache, validation, the coverage report, "Why unsupported?" and the unsupported flags stay unchanged. An unsupported card is still flagged and still blocks play; the dialog now tells the player to replace it. An existing browser database may still hold an unused `requests` object store (and an unused `overrides` store, from the community definitions removed in D-167): nothing reads them, and the schema version stays 2 (new databases create neither).
- Alternatives: Keep a manual "Copy for agent" button and drop only the inbox and the CLI: rejected by the owner: the message and the schema behind it are most of the code, and the owner no longer wants the request step. Keep the tracking of open and resolved requests per browser: rejected, it needs the same store and the reconcile step for a list nobody reads. Remove the diagnostics too (`stoppedAt`, `closestRule`, `reason`, `needs`): rejected, "Why unsupported?" and `reports/backlog.md` use them.
- Consequences: The card support loop starts from an issue or from the owner's list; the playbook says where the Oracle text and the blockers come from instead. The sections of `docs/SPEC.md` about support requests (section 10 "Support requests" and "Request support", `CardSupportRequest` in the schema list of 17.6, the loop's milestone lines) are history until the owner approves a SPEC change. D-054 is superseded; D-064 and D-040 carry a note. The Korvold request file that `card-requests/done/` held is gone; its text lives in the golden corpus, and older design notes that name that path are history. D-167 and D-168 merged first, so the shared web import code (the import environment, the IndexedDB stores and the import screen) lost the requests and the community definitions together; neither feature exists any more.

## D-167: Remove the community definitions (2026-10-30)
- Context: The owner simplified the product: the community card definitions (D-067, D-071, D-080) were a second route to support a card, as reviewed JSON files pinned to the Oracle text, with a registry, a bundle step in the web build, a loader in the app, a "Card definitions" tab, a "community" badge and two roadmap steps (a builder, and export and contribute). No definition was ever shipped, and every card already goes through the parser or an engine fixture.
- Decision: No community definitions. Removed: `card-definitions/`, `packages/cards/src/definitions/` (file schema, registry, text pin, overrides adapter), `tools/definitions/` and `pnpm definitions:bundle` (and its run by the web `dev` and `build` scripts), the loader, the manager, the IndexedDB store and the tab of the web app, the "community" support source and badge, and roadmap steps 2 and 3. Kept: deck import (decklist parsing, the Scryfall client and cache, validation, the coverage section and "Why unsupported?"), the unsupported-card flagging (a card the parser does not fully support stays unsupported), the engine's real-card fixtures and the SYNTHETIC test fixtures. `SPEC.md` is not edited here; its mentions wait for the owner's approval.
- Alternatives: Keep the pipeline dormant, without a UI or files: rejected, it is dead code that the tests, the docs and the support cache key would still carry. Keep only the shipped-files half and drop the paste-in-the-browser half: rejected, nothing ships and the half that stays would still need the registry, the bundle and the loader.
- Consequences: The only way to support a card is a parser rule or an engine primitive (the O class of the support playbook has no route: such a card stays unsupported). The override mechanism was not only for definitions, so its core stays: `OverrideRegistry` and `createFixtureRegistry` are how the engine's real-card fixtures reach `importCard` (a fixture is used only when it agrees with the real card; a stale one blocks, D-052), `DEFAULT_OVERRIDES` is what the web app, `pnpm card:request` and `pnpm ai:arena --precons` pass, and the golden corpus, the grammar and the layout tests pass an empty fixture registry (`NO_OVERRIDES`) to see the parser alone. Removed from that mechanism because only definitions used it: `composeOverrides`, `createCommunityOverrides`, `OverrideRegistry.identity`, `SupportReport.definitionKey` and `notes`, the sources `community` and the never-produced `override`, and the `ready` option of the import service. `cachedSupport` now also recomputes a cached report that still carries a `definitionKey`, so a browser that cached a card as supported through a definition does not keep trusting it. The IndexedDB version stays 2 so existing databases still open; a browser that has the `overrides` store keeps it, unused, and new databases do not create it. `golden.expected.json` is unchanged.

## D-168: Remove the Easy level of the AI (2026-10-30)
- Context: The owner simplified the product and decided to drop the Easy mode. D-163 gave `HeuristicAgent` a `level` (`'normal' | 'easy'`, Easy with at most three candidates, no windows, the casual mana play and a one in four second-best choice) and D-164 put an Easy and Normal setting on the menu and the import screen, stored in the browser. On the real precons Easy was about even with the old casual opponent (52.5% and 42.5% in 40 games each, D-164 finding 2), so it was not clearly easier than what players had before; it was only simpler than Normal.
- Decision: There is one AI level: `HeuristicAgent` as it played at Normal. The `level` option, every Easy-only branch (the candidate caps of the block and attack choice, the second-best draw, the casual-style priority play, the removal-aiming switch), the `Level` type, the `heuristic-easy` factory of `AGENT_FACTORIES` and of `pnpm ai:arena` are gone. In the web the setting and its storage are gone (`AiLevelPicker.tsx`, `ui/panels/ai-level.ts`, the `commander-arena.ai-level` key, the hint lines): the menu and "Play this deck" send `ai: 'normal'`. `NewGameOptions.ai` stays and is `'casual' | 'normal'`; `?autostart=...&ai=casual|normal` stays for the tests and the default stays `casual`; a stale `&ai=easy` names no agent and plays as the default. Normal's play is unchanged: the same decisions for the same seed (the Easy branches never read the agent's PRNG at Normal), checked with the unit tests of the agent and with `node tools/ai/arena.ts --a heuristic --b greedy --games 20 --seed 1` before and after (same wins, turns and reason histogram). The agent's name is now `heuristic#<seed>` (it was `heuristic-normal#<seed>`). The precon soak test of `tools/ai` plays `heuristic` against `casual` now (it played `heuristic-easy`).
- Alternatives: Keeping a hidden Easy (`?ai=easy`, `heuristic-easy` in the arena): rejected, it is dead code that the tests would have to keep paying for, and a level nobody can choose.
- Consequences: The tuning and the measurements of D-163 apply to the only level. D-163 and D-164 keep their text, with a status note; the Easy numbers in them and in `docs/progress/M7.md` are history. SPEC 9 ("Difficulty levels: Easy and Normal") and SPEC 10 ("Game settings: difficulty") are history too (the SPEC is changed only with the owner's approval). A harder or easier level can come back later as a new decision, with a measured gap.

## D-169: Collapse the SPEC into a short current specification (2026-11-01)
- Context: `docs/SPEC.md` was about 600 lines: the original specification plus 31 amendments (A1 to A31) and milestones M0 to M10. After the simplification (D-165 to D-168) and the end of M7 it described removed features as planned or in place (saves and replays, the support-request pipeline, community definitions, overrides files, the Easy level, the Easy and Normal difficulty, the stronger AI as future work), and a reader had to apply the amendments to the sections by hand. The owner approved collapsing it, and trimming `docs/PRIOR_ART.md` alongside (2026-10-30 and 2026-11-01).
- Decision: `docs/SPEC.md` is now a short statement of the current product: purpose and scope (with the removed features listed as removed), priorities, the architecture and engine requirements with the amendments folded in, card data and the support status (supported or unsupported, never partial), the AI (`HeuristicAgent`, the 1 s budget, what it may know, A31), the UI as it exists, legal and API etiquette in full, the quality bar with the 30 required scenario tests and the property and soak tests, the repository documents, a milestone status table (M0 to M7 done with pointers to `docs/progress/`, M8 and M9 built as slices with the performance budgets left, M10 and M11 not started) and the definition of done. The numbered top-level sections 1 to 17 and the sub-numbering that code, tests and documents cite (4.1 to 4.3, 5.1 to 5.9, 6.1, 6.2, 7.1 to 7.3, 8.1 to 8.4, 17.1 to 17.7) are kept. Where a cited section no longer applies (8.2 and 8.4 on support requests, scenario test 30) the heading stays with a line saying it was removed and which decision did it. Section 17 is an amendments index: one line per amendment A1 to A31, saying what it decided and either "now in section X" or the decision that removed or superseded it; the amendment text is not kept. `docs/PRIOR_ART.md` keeps the sources read, their licenses and the reuse limits (GPL ideas only, attributions), what was studied, the AI findings of 7.2 with the ranked heuristics and where `HeuristicAgent` implements each, the XMage scenario list of 7.3, 7.5 and the token notes of 7.6; the survey rows and the recommendations for M7 that nothing uses are gone. `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` and `docs/STATUS.md` point at the new structure.
- Alternatives: Deleting the amendments outright: rejected, hundreds of comments, tests and documents cite "SPEC 17.1 A5", "A28", "SPEC 7.1" and so on, and every such citation would break. Keeping the amendments in full under the short sections: rejected, it keeps the size and the contradictions. Rewriting the citations in `packages/` and `apps/`: rejected, it is a large diff across code for no gain while the numbers resolve.
- Consequences: A new session reads one short document for the current product, and the history stays in `docs/DECISIONS.md`. Section and amendment numbers must not be renumbered: new content goes under an existing number or a new number at the end. Some code comments cite A29 where A31 is meant (the AI sample, D-161): the index resolves A29 to the unsupported-deck rule, so those comments are stale and should say A31 when next touched. No code, test or behavior changed.

## D-170: A lone blocker goes on the attacker it kills, in the block plan and in the opponent model (2026-11-01)
- Context: Issue 73, a game the owner lost against the web opponent (D-163, D-164, D-168). In the opponent's turn 9 the agent attacked with its commander Giada, Font of Hope (a 2/2 flier with vigilance) and Youthful Valkyrie (3/5 flier) into the human's one untapped creature that could block fliers, Scrapshooter (4/4 reach). Scrapshooter blocked Giada, killed her, and she went back to the command zone. The owner asked whether the attack had any good reason.
- Diagnosis (reproduced with the real cards of the precon snapshots, built through the web import pipeline and placed with the scenario DSL: AI at 14 life with Giada, Valkyrie 3/5 and a summoning-sick Angel of Finality; human at 9 with Scrapshooter and Llanowar Elves untapped and Rhonas and Yeva tapped; the agent chose both fliers with reason `sim-attack`, as in the log). The scored candidates before the fix (weight of the passive opponent 0.5, the prior; `raw`, `crack`, `dealt` as in `heuristic-attacks.ts`; the careful play is against the sensible opponent): stay home raw -1.21, crack 0.47; Valkyrie alone raw -1.81 (blocked for nothing); Giada alone, careful raw -7.73 (she dies; the evaluator charges her whole body, about 6.5 points), passive raw +2.74; both, careful raw +2.14, crack 2.65, dealt 2, passive the same. So the sensible opponent of the simulation never killed Giada in the pair. The cause is `Planner.good` in `heuristic-blockplan.ts`: it walks the attackers strongest first by `creatureValue` and gives each the cheapest blocker that survives, killing when that blocker can. With one reach blocker and two fliers it gave Scrapshooter to Valkyrie (it survives, no kill) and had none left for Giada, which it would have killed, so the simulated block stopped 3 damage and the commander lived. The same planner chooses the agent's own blocks (as tier 1 of `blockPlans`) and stands in for the opponent when an attack is played out (`defaultPlan`), so the fault had two faces. The hypotheses of the issue brief: (a) the evaluator treats the commander's death as cheap: no, it removes the whole body and gives the command zone nothing, so the death was priced at about 6.5 points and the evaluator is, if anything, generous to the attack; (b) the opponent model learned passivity: the run above used the prior (0.5) and the passive play of the pair is a legitimate mix, so the model only matters for how much of the careful play counts; (c) the library clock: urgency was 0 in the reproduction (30 cards in each library; the real libraries of the log were not recorded, so this is not shown for the game itself); (d) Scrapshooter's reach not read: it was read (the simulated opponent did block a flier with it); by the code the safe-attacker test (`survivesAttack`) leaves Giada out of the "safe attackers" candidate (not printed), so the pair came from the "every attacker" candidate, scored with the faulty block; (e) the lethal check: not lethal (5 damage against 9 life). So the owner is right: the attack had no good reason. It gained only what Valkyrie's attack gains, and it put the commander in front of a blocker that kills her for free; the agent attacked because its model of the human blocked the wrong creature.
- Decision: `Planner.good` makes two passes: the blocks that survive and kill first (strongest attacker first, the cheapest such blocker), then the blocks that only survive, for the attackers still open. No card name, no number: the planner reads the same duel results as before. Tests first (`heuristic-blocks.test.ts`, `heuristic-attacks.test.ts`): a 3/5 flier and a 2/2 flier attacking into one 4/4 reach blocker are blocked as the 2/2 (with and without a sample); the attack of the issue with synthetic cards of the same shape (a 2/2 flying vigilance commander, a 3/5 flier, a 3/4 flier that is summoning sick; a 4/4 reach blocker and two big tapped creatures on the other side) keeps the commander home (it failed before the fix, with the commander going); and a commander at 20 life does not chump block a bigger attacker. The evaluator is not changed (see (a)); no constant was changed.
- Same flaw in blocks? Yes, the planner is shared, so the agent's own blocks had it: with fewer blockers than attackers it could spend a blocker on the strongest attacker it only stops and let a killable one through (the candidate plans are scored by play-out, but none of them put the blocker on the killable attacker unless the danger fill happened to). The fix covers it. Blocks with the commander were checked in the code and in a test: the commander is a creature like any other there (it blocks when it survives, trades when the attacker is worth as much and chumps only in danger); nothing in the agent names a commander except the commander-tax rule of the main phase.
- Measured (code of `origin/main` at `05dba63` against the fix, the same commands on the same machine, run at the same time, so the loaded machine is the same for both; each 200 games are 100 seeds played twice with the seats swapped, logical clock, no fallback, no rejected action, no draw and no unfinished game in any run). `node tools/ai/arena.ts --a heuristic --b greedy --games 200 --seed 1`: 181 wins (90.5%) before, 180 (90.0%) after; `--seed 2`: 184 (92.0%) before, 184 (92.0%) after; `--a heuristic --b random --seed 1`: 200 before and after; `--a heuristic --b casual --seed 1`: 123 (61.5%) before and after. The numbers before equal those of D-163. The A11 targets (70% against Greedy, 95% against Random) stay met. Precons, `node tools/ai/arena.ts --precons --pairing cross --a heuristic --b casual --games 40 --seed 1 --real-clock`: 22 of 40 (55.0%) before, 23 of 40 (57.5%) after (standard error of 40 games about 8 points); slowest heuristic decision 701.4 ms before and 706.3 ms after (mean 3.5 ms in both), none over the 1000 ms budget; both runs shared the machine.
- Alternatives: Playing out every candidate block plan of the opponent and scoring the attack against its best answer: the principled answer to "the opponent blocks as well as it can", rejected for now because it multiplies the play-outs of every attack candidate (the budget of D-164 was found on boards where one play-out took seconds). A commander-death surcharge in the evaluator (tax, tempo): rejected, the evaluator already charges the whole body and gives the command zone nothing, so a surcharge would make the commander worth more than any other creature without a measured reason; the recast cost is a tempo that the evaluator does not see for any creature. Treating a commander as unsafe to attack with whenever a blocker could kill it: rejected, it is a card-type special case, and the scored attack already holds it back once the block is modelled right. Making the model less passive after one seen block: not needed, the fix does not depend on it.
- Consequences: The simulated opponent now puts a lone blocker where it kills, so attacks that offered a free kill look as bad as they are, and the agent's blocks take the kill it was missing. The remaining limit is that the opponent is still modelled by one plan per kind (sensible or in danger only), not by its best answer among all plans (ROADMAP). In the position of the issue the agent now stays home (reason `crack-back`: its best raw score was still the double attack, held back by the crack-back penalty, 8.36 careful against 0.47 at home), which means the margin that protects the commander there is the crack-back, not the raw evaluation (careful raw of the pair -0.43 against -1.21 at home). No `ENGINE_VERSION` change: no rule changed.

## D-172: The AI gets 5 s a decision, the other performance budgets stay (2026-11-01)
- Context: The owner asked to increase just the AI budget and not the others, and said that 5 s may be fine. In a real Commander game a person takes minutes a turn, so waiting a few seconds for the AI costs nothing. The `HeuristicAgent` scores candidate plays until it has used 60% of its budget (D-163, D-164), so more budget means more candidates scored and better play on big boards, and a phone or an old laptop, several times slower than the dev machine, cuts the search early with a tight budget. SPEC 9 and 12 said 1 s a decision (SPEC 17.6 A28 is the watchdog that enforces it).
- Decision: `DEFAULT_BUDGET_MS` in `packages/ai/src/agent.ts` is 5000 (was 1000). The A28 watchdog margin `DEFAULT_MARGIN_MS` in `apps/web/src/game/host.ts` is 2500 ms (was 500 ms), the same 50% of the budget as before, so the host replaces an answer that takes more than 7500 ms (budget plus margin; was 1500 ms) with the safe fallback and counts it. The agent's own shares are fractions of `ctx.budgetMs` and are unchanged: the search stops at 60% (now 3000 ms) and a running play-out is dropped at 70% (now 3500 ms). `aiBudgetMs` and `aiMarginMs` of the host stay as options, and a caller that sets one is not affected. SPEC 9 and 12 say 5 s, with the reason. The other budgets are unchanged: `applyAction` under 5 ms, `getLegalActions` under 20 ms, animations at 60 fps.
- Alternatives: A user setting for the budget: rejected for now, one number is simpler and nobody asked for the choice. Loosening the engine budgets too: rejected, they bound the cost of the AI's look-ahead (every play-out is many `applyAction` calls) and the CI time, and the owner asked for the AI budget only. Keeping the margin at 500 ms: rejected, the margin was 50% of the budget, and 500 ms would be 10% of a 5 s budget.
- Consequences: The budget is a cap, not a delay: a typical decision still takes milliseconds (the arena run below has a mean of a few ms), and only a decision on a big board can use up to the 60% share, 3 s, plus the rest of its answer. The worst case for one AI turn is a few such decisions in a row. The web page has no "opponent is thinking" indicator: the store's `busy` flag drives only the `data-settled` attribute that the browser tests wait for, the action bar prints "Waiting for the game." when it has no decision to show, and the "Opponent is ..." line exists only for the engine's `waitingOn` purposes (search, discard, scry and so on). The page also receives the snapshot only after the host's AI run has finished. So a long decision looks like a pause; a visible state is a possible follow-up listed in `docs/ROADMAP.md` and not built. Measured on one machine that other jobs also used, one run each, code of `origin/main` at `677abca` against this change: `node tools/ai/arena.ts --precons --pairing cross --a heuristic --b casual --games 40 --seed 1 --real-clock --log-slow 1000`: main 23 wins of 40 for `heuristic`, mean 3.61 ms, slowest 628.8 ms, no decision over 1000 ms; this change 22 wins, mean 3.67 ms, slowest 1445.0 ms, three decisions over 1000 ms (1445.0, 1224.5 and 1084.1 ms, all declare-attackers). With a real clock the agent may score more candidates when it has more time, so the real-clock win counts can differ a little between the two; one run of 40 games cannot tell a change in strength from noise. `node tools/ai/arena.ts --a heuristic --b greedy --games 200 --seed 1` (logical clock): the same on both, 180 wins to 20 for `heuristic`, 56039 decisions, the same reason histogram.

## D-173: A cheaper `derive` for big boards, with the results kept per state (2026-11-01)
- Context: M7d (D-164) found that on the real 100-card precons a board reaches 50 to 80 permanents and that the static-effect derivation (`rules/derive*.ts`) dominates the profile: one candidate play-out of the `HeuristicAgent` took 2.4 s and the slowest decisions were 700 to 870 ms against the budget. The performance budgets of SPEC 12 (`applyAction` under 5 ms, `getLegalActions` under 20 ms) are an owner-kept M9 leftover. The task was a pure speed-up: the same derived characteristics, legal actions, state hashes and events, no `ENGINE_VERSION` change (still 35), no change to the AI.
- Measured before (the benchmark `node tools/perf/derive-bench.ts`, new in this change: the five precons through the web import pipeline, `CasualAgent` games to turn 40 or the end, the biggest board of each of 40 seeds kept, timed on fresh `structuredClone` copies so no cache keyed by a state can be warm; the four boards kept had 58, 55, 52 and 49 permanents). The numbers before and after are in "Measured after". A profile (`node --cpu-prof`) of those games: `derive` was 60% of all CPU time and 90% of the time inside `applyAction`; the garbage collector 14%; `printedValues` (it copied the face of the card with a rest spread on every call) 7.7% self time. What the profile showed, in order: (1) `derive` is called for the same permanent many times for one state: one `applyAction` ends in `priorityOptions`, which for each activatable ability and each castable spell asks `planFor`, which asks `paymentSources`, which derives every permanent. Over 111 actions of one of those games (actions 450 to 561 of seed 127) there were 60 389 calls of `derive` for 11 399 distinct (state, object) pairs, 5.3 times as many; (2) each fresh `derive` rescanned the continuous effects of the game several times (`effectsOn` filtered the whole list for each caller: the copiable values, the type layers, `finish`), rebuilt the static-ability lists and conditions' JSON keys of the board index, expanded keywords again, and counted (`countForSource`) for every permanent and every counted amount; (3) several rules (player protection, the hand size, extra land drops, triggered mana abilities, Aura checks) derived every permanent only to look for one kind of ability or for the subtypes.
- Decision: results are kept where the answer is a pure function of values that are never changed in place, keyed by the identity of exactly those values, and never longer than the value lives (`WeakMap`, no size to manage, nothing global to reset). Nothing else changed: no rule, no AST, no card. (a) `derive(state, obj)` keeps its answer per (state, object) (`rules/derive.ts`), `typeViewOf` per (state, object) (`derive-view.ts`), `countForSource` per (state, filter, source) (`derive-count.ts`) and `paymentSources` per (state, seat) (`mana-sources.ts`). A new game state is a new object with every change (`state/ops.ts`: `setObject`, `patchObject` and the spreads of the rules copy; nothing mutates a state or an object in place, a grep and the whole engine suite agree), and an object that changes is a new object, so the pair (state, object) is a key that cannot go stale: the cache holds nothing the pair does not determine, and a state that is built another way (the scenario DSL, `determinize`, `structuredClone`) is just a new key. The result is read-only (`Derived` is `readonly` throughout) and shared by the callers. (b) Things that depend on less are kept on less: the printed values of a card face, of a token definition and the combined values of a split card by their (immutable) definition (`copiable.ts`), the keyword expansion and the static modifiers of an ability list by the list (`derive-keywords.ts`, `derive-statics.ts`: the JSON key of a condition is made once instead of once per index), the continuous effects grouped per object and the set of objects that lost all abilities by the effects list, which most states share (`derive-layers.ts`, `lost-abilities.ts`), the filter of a subject that says "other" and the context a static ability's filter reads of its permanent by the subject and by the board index (`static-subject.ts`, `derive-statics.ts`). (c) The board index lists the static abilities that name "this" or "the attached permanent" under that permanent, so they are tried for it alone, in the same order (a sequence number is kept and the lists are merged by it; D-111 and D-149 ordering is unchanged). (d) A rule that scans the battlefield for one kind of static ability first asks `mayHaveStatic` (`rules/printed-statics.ts`): derived abilities are the copiable abilities with their keyword expansions, plus keywords, the expansions of Exalted and Prowess, the abilities a `grantAbility` gives (mana, activated or triggered, never static) and alternative-cost abilities (triggered or keyword); "loses all abilities" only removes; so an object whose copiable abilities and expansions hold no static of the kind cannot have one after any layer, and `derive` is skipped. A "maybe" still derives. (e) The Aura and attachment checks of the state-based actions read `typeViewOf` for the subtypes and types: they are what layers 1, 4 and 5 leave, which `derive` copies unchanged.
- Proof that nothing changed. (1) A differential test, `packages/engine/test/derive-differential.test.ts` (helpers `derive-digest.ts`, recorded file `derive-digest.expected.json`): nine seeded random games are played step by step (three on decks of static-heavy synthetic cards, one on the combat decks, five from boards built with the scenario DSL that start with 70 permanents: lords, anthems, Auras, Equipment, copy effects, "loses all abilities" and conditions on both sides). At every step it fingerprints the derived characteristics (including restrictions, block limits and attachments) of every object not in a library and the legal actions; every fifth step both players' views, every tenth the state hash. The fingerprints were recorded with the unchanged engine, then before each change they were required to come out the same; a second test fingerprints the recorded states again backwards and interleaved, so an answer that depends on what was asked before fails; a third checks that the games really exercise statics (changed power, attachments, restrictions). On the old code the file takes 73 s (the boards of 70 permanents are what is slow), on the new 15 s. (2) A key test, `derive-cache-keys.test.ts`: states built to differ in exactly one thing (the same object table with another list of continuous effects, or another battlefield; the same state with another object; an anthem that changed controller; type views and counts; payment sources and seats). The differential test alone did not catch a derive cache keyed by the object table, so this was added; mutation checks (a scratch edit, then restored): `derive` keyed by the object only (fails 3 tests of the key test and the differential), by the object table (2 key tests fail), `countForSource` keyed by the battlefield (1), `typeViewOf` keyed by the object table (1), `paymentSources` keyed by the object table (1) and one that ignores the seat (1). (3) `node tools/perf/precon-digest.ts --games 10` (new; real precons through the web pipeline, `RandomLegalAgent`, about 12 000 steps of views, legal actions and state hashes through the public API) printed the same ten lines on `origin/main` and on this branch. (4) `pnpm exec vitest run packages/engine --exclude "**/scenario-xx-combat-random-games*"` passes unchanged, and so do the AI, cards (golden corpus) and tools tests. (5) The arena: with the logical clock `node tools/ai/arena.ts --a heuristic --b greedy --games 200 --seed 1` prints the same output on both (180 wins, 20, the same reason histogram, 56 039 decisions); with the real clock on the precons (40 games, seed 1) 22 wins to 18 on both, cross and mirror, with the same number of decisions.
- Measured after (the same benchmark, run after the old code on the same machine, twice in turn; the machine is shared, so the numbers vary about 15% between runs; the first pair is shown, the second gave a whole turn of 2362 ms before and 583 ms after, a mean `applyAction` of 21.3 and 5.3 ms). On the 58-permanent board, `applyAction` over the 111 actions of the turn: mean 20.7 to 4.5 ms, p99 50.5 to 17.0 ms, slowest 75.0 to 25.5 ms; the whole turn 2293 to 504 ms (4.5 times faster); its combat steps 460 to 100 ms; `getView` of a new state 15.7 to 3.1 ms (the second call on the same state 14.9 to 0.9 ms); the first five legal actions applied to the state, `applyAction` mean 13.5 to 5.1 ms. On the other boards kept (55, 52 and 49 permanents) the same five actions: 14.7 to 6.1, 7.6 to 3.2 and 3.3 to 2.0 ms. `getLegalActions` was 0.01 to 0.04 ms before and after: it returns the options the previous `applyAction` already built into the pending decision, so the cost of listing the legal plays is inside `applyAction`.
- The AI check (same machine, one run after the other, `--real-clock --log-slow 700`, origin/main at `7e6adfa` against this branch merged with it): `--precons --pairing cross --a heuristic --b casual --games 40 --seed 1`: wins 22 to 18 on both; mean decision time of the heuristic agent 3.33 to 1.19 ms, slowest 1162.4 to 349.6 ms, decisions over 700 ms 4 to 0, 8549 decisions on both, the run 88.8 s to 35.8 s. `--pairing mirror`: wins 22 to 18 on both; mean 3.93 to 1.35 ms, slowest 1162.6 to 437.1 ms, over 700 ms 9 to 0, the run 125 s to 47 s. No decision came near the 5 s budget (D-172) on either, so the agent's own time cut-off (60% of the budget, 3 s) cannot have fired in these runs, which is why the games are the same; where it does fire (boards of 70 or more permanents, a slower machine) the agent now gets through more of its candidates before it. Logical clock, `--a heuristic --b greedy --games 200 --seed 1`: mean 2.63 to 0.87 ms, slowest 255.1 to 97.1 ms, the run 5 min 21 s to 1 min 48 s.
- SPEC 12 budgets on these boards, honestly: `applyAction` mean is 4.5 ms (5.3 ms in the second run) on the 58-permanent turn and 2.0 to 6.1 ms on the single actions measured, so the mean is at the 5 ms budget on a board that size and under it on the others, but the p99 over that turn is 17 to 21 ms and the slowest action 26 to 34 ms (a priority pass that resolves a stack or starts a step, a land play, ordering triggers), so the "under 5 ms" budget is missed in the tail of big boards. `getLegalActions` is far under 20 ms (0.01 to 0.04 ms) because the options are built by `applyAction` and read back. `getView` of a new state is 3 ms. The budgets stay an M9 leftover for the tail.
- What is left: `derive` is still about a quarter of the CPU time of a game on these boards. Every new state derives every permanent once more (the callers that need the abilities of all permanents: `paymentSources`, the triggered mana abilities, `objectView`, `collectTriggers`), because each change of the game, even tapping a land, is a new state and a new object table; the board index of static abilities and the group-type index are rebuilt for each object table (a few percent each).
- Alternatives: A cache across states of the whole `derive` result, valid while the object and the "environment" are the same: rejected. What a derived characteristic reads of the other objects (counts by filter, conditions, linked exile, attachments, tapped status, counters) is open-ended in the AST, and the object table is copied on every `patchObject`, so deciding that a tap of a land cannot change an unrelated permanent needs a per-field dependency analysis of every ability a deck can have; a wrong answer is a silent rules bug, and the differential test could not prove it for cards it does not contain. Derived fields computed on demand (power and toughness only when read): rejected, layer 7 amounts and the grants are one interleaved pass whose order is the result (D-111, D-149); splitting it risks a change of order for a gain on the callers that read only abilities. A persistent map for `GameState.objects` so a patch does not copy the table: rejected here, it changes every access to the table. Memoizing `planFor` or `priorityOptions`: rejected, the options differ with the cost and the sacrifice and reserve arguments and the cache key would be the whole argument list; memoizing its inputs (`paymentSources`) does the same work for less. Weakening the guard that the output is byte-identical to make a bigger change: not done.
- Consequences: A big board costs a few times less in `applyAction` and `getView`, so the AI's look-ahead and the page both have headroom, and the time cut-off of the agent fires later. Every rule that reads `derive` gets its answer from a cache keyed by the identity of the state and the object: a new rule must not mutate a state or an object in place (it never did), and a function that wants a cached answer for less than the state (as `effectsOn` and the printed values do) must read nothing else; the key test is where to add the case. The benchmark and the precon digest live in `tools/perf` and read a real clock, which is allowed there. `docs/ROADMAP.md` keeps what is left.

## D-174: An "Opponent is thinking" status, inferred from the page's own request (2026-11-02)
- Context: With a 5 s AI budget (D-172) a long decision on a big board looks like a pause: the page has no sign that anything is happening. The owner asked for an indicator and approved the one clause in SPEC 10. The Worker answers once, after the player's action and the AI's whole run (`GameHost.act` awaits `runAi`), so the page sees no partial progress. The store's `busy` flag cannot be the signal: it also covers the pause before an automatic pass, the undo and the whole autopilot chain, which are many quick requests in a row.
- Decision: no protocol change. (1) `AppState.hostCall` in `store.ts` is the number of the `client.act` request in flight, or null: set by one wrapper (`callAct`) that the player's action and the autopilot's passes both use, cleared when that request ends (a request that was replaced by a later one does not clear the later one). Undo and `newGame` do not set it: undo never runs the AI, and `newGame` is shown as "Shuffling…". (2) `ui/decisions/thinking.ts`: `watchThinking(store, delayMs, onChange, timers)` tells whether a request has lasted `THINKING_DELAY_MS` = 400 ms, from its own start (each request counts again from zero, so a chain of quick passes never adds up), and false the instant the request ends or the game is over; `useOpponentThinking(delayMs = THINKING_DELAY_MS)` wraps it for React. The timer is `setTimeout`, so tests drive it with fake timers; no clock is read in render. (3) `DecisionLayer` passes the flag to `ActionBar`, which draws a `.dec-thinking` line, `role="status"` and `aria-live="polite"`, reading "Opponent is thinking" and three dots that fade in turn (a static state under `prefers-reduced-motion`). The line is always in the bar and always one line tall (`min-height` of one line at `--text-scale`, D-141), empty when the opponent is not thinking, so showing it moves nothing in the dock: the dock keeps its bottom edge and its box in both states (checked with the browser test and with screenshots at 1280 by 720 and 1366 by 768, Large, and 1280 by 720, Normal). The reserved line makes the dock one line taller than before, always. Nothing is added to the game log, which stays the record of game events.
- Why this signal: a `client.act` request is the human's action, which the engine applies in milliseconds (the mean `applyAction` is 2 to 6 ms on big boards, D-173), plus the AI's run. A request that lasts 400 ms is therefore the AI deciding, and the page needs nothing from the host. Known inexact cases: (a) a request that is slow for another reason, such as the engine on a big board on a slow machine, shows the same status; (b) while a modal question is on screen (a mulligan, a card picker; `bar.inOverlay`) the dock is hidden, so the status is not shown, and that modal stays until the answer arrives; (c) `newGame` (the opponent's opening decisions) shows "Shuffling…", not the status.
- Test seam: `?autostart=...&aidelay=<ms>` (`game/slow-opponent.ts`, wired in `main.tsx`) wraps the Worker client on the page's side and holds back every answer in which the AI acted for that many milliseconds. It is read only when the URL has `?autostart`, needs a whole number from 1 up (capped at 10 000), and changes nothing for the engine, the host or a game started from the menu. The Playwright test `e2e/thinking.e2e.ts` uses it.
- Alternatives: A progress callback from the host with the AI's partial results (a Comlink callback or a second message): rejected for now, it is a protocol change and a new race (callbacks arriving after the answer) for a status line that the page can infer; it would be the way to show what the AI considers. `aiThinking` marked in the snapshot: rejected, the snapshot is sent only after the run, so it would say nothing during it. A line in the game log: rejected, the log is the record of game events and a thinking line would be a fake event (and would have to be taken back). A spinner on the pass button or a dimmed board: rejected, the buttons are not the opponent's, and dimming moves attention. Replacing the prompt text by the status: rejected, a prompt of two lines would change the dock's height. Showing it at once: rejected, a quick move would flash the line.
- Consequences: A long AI decision is visible and announced politely to screen readers, quick moves show nothing, and the dock does not move. `busy` and `data-settled` are unchanged, so the browser tests wait as before. The 400 ms constant is a guess at the shortest wait a player notices, not a measurement. D-172 said the page had no indicator; this entry replaces that remark, and the follow-up bullet is gone from `docs/ROADMAP.md`.

## D-175: The Korvold slice, text and tokens, engine: one of several instructions chosen as an effect resolves, "dies" for every permanent, and Choose a Background (2026-11-02)
- Context: The owner's Korvold deck has 45 cards the engine did not run (`docs/proposals/korvold-deck-analysis.md`); slice 1 is twelve of them that the analysis called text and tokens (parser only, "no engine to a few lines"). Each was run through today's parser and `validateCard` before planning (the pipeline reports only the first unread piece of a line), which found three engine facts, listed under Decision. The class calls of the analysis moved: Tireless Provisioner's "create a Food token or a Treasure token" was T and is P (an inline choice the engine had no node for); Rancor's "When ~ is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, return it to its owner's hand" was T and is P (the engine's `died` event was emitted for creatures only, against CR 700.4); Ganax's "Choose a Background" was K and stays K. The Mending of Dominaria (a whole graveyard to a library), the quoted abilities of tokens, "a number of tapped Treasure tokens equal to its power", Gilt-Leaf's Embrace, Temur Battle Rage, My Precious's Equip and Cindervines needed no engine change: the engine already ran what the parser lowers (proved by `convert-grammar-engine-p35.test.ts`).
- Decision: (1) **`chooseOne` effect** (`Effect` `{ kind: 'chooseOne', options: { label, effect }[] }`, `rules/choose-one.ts`, instruction `chooseOne`): the controller of the resolving spell or ability chooses one of two to eight instructions as it comes up (CR 608.2d: a choice an effect offers is made while the effect is applied; it is not a mode, CR 700.2, which is chosen as the spell or ability goes on the stack). The question is a `chooseOption` decision with the new `purpose` `'effect'`, whose options are the labels in order; the answer runs that option's effect and nothing else; the event `optionChosen` (purpose `'effect'`) logs it. `validateCard` checks two to eight options, labels that are not empty and differ, and each option as any effect (`ast/validate-parts.ts`, `ast/supported.ts`). Feature `effect:chooseOne`. (2) **"Dies" is any permanent** (`rules/zones.ts`): the `died` event is emitted when any permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, as CR 700.4 says ("The term dies means 'is put into a graveyard from the battlefield'"); the engine had read it as a creature put there, and so a trigger on an Aura or an artifact dying never fired. A trigger for "a creature that dies" is unchanged (it reads the types the permanent had on the battlefield, CR 603.10a). (3) **Keyword `chooseBackground`** (CR 702.124k): a deck-construction ability with no effect in the game, as `partner`; `validateCard` accepts it, `derive` expands it into nothing, and `packages/cards` already read it for the pair of commanders (D-053). (4) **AI and web.** `CasualAgent` answers `purpose` `'effect'` by the words of the options (a Treasure, then a card, else the first listed; the decision names no more than the words, `casual-options.ts`); `RandomLegalAgent` takes any listed option. The web draws it with the dialog of the named options (`NamedOptionDialog`, titled "Choose one", one capitalised button for each instruction, no way out), the prompt "Choose one for X: a or b.", and the log line "You choose to create a Food token (X)." (CR 608.2d). `ENGINE_VERSION` is 36.
